blocks.html:
In Short
  • What I Owned: Act II gameplay and puzzles end to end, Act II camera and controls, and the playtest process. I also co-defined the 3C for the whole game.
  • Hardest Problem: A puzzle players couldn't see. Reframing the camera, sightlines and lighting raised its solve rate from ~70% to ~90%.
  • What it Shows: Designing for players who have never held a controller, teaching without text, and turning playtest observations into specific changes.

• A team of 6 with no dedicated QA, so the designers planned and ran playtesting themselves.
  • About nine months from start to release.
  • An all-ages audience: many players had little experience with 3D movement or camera control.
  • No text tutorials, by choice: the story is told without words, so tutorial text would break it.

blocks.html:
1. Feel Before Challenge: movement and camera have to feel right before any puzzle can be fair.
  2. Show, Don't Tell: the game teaches through space, motion and discovery, not text.
  3. Gentle Mastery: puzzles grow from intuition to insight, and failing never punishes the player.

In a narrative game, how it feels is the first impression. Before a puzzle can be fair or a story can land, players have to trust how the character moves and how the camera shows the space. I co-defined the 3C with the design team, and designed the camera and controls for Act II.

The camera's job is to reveal the puzzle, not fight it.

  • Framing that Hints at the Goal: Default angles keep the next objective in view, so the space suggests where to go.
  • Smooth, Predictable Follow: No sudden snaps or fast rotation, to avoid motion sickness in players new to 3D.
  • Composed Angles for Story Moments: Fixed or guided shots where the story needs them.

For an all-ages audience, the controls have to turn what the player means into what the character does.

  • Generous Tolerances: Wider interaction ranges and forgiving collision, so near-misses count.
  • Gentle Assists: Coyote time and auto-alignment to interactable objects.
  • Readable Animation: The character's pose shows clearly what state it's in and what it can do next.

The aim was that failing feels like learning, never like fighting the controls.

blocks.html: I owned the gameplay of the whole second act: its structure, its puzzles, and how each space teaches the player something new. I refined the blockouts with level design so the spaces guide players without hand-holding.
Act II alternates puzzle spaces with quiet story moments, so challenge never runs long enough to tire young players, and emotional beats land when the player has room to feel them.

Each mechanic follows the same four steps, so Act II needs no text tutorials:

  1. Introduce it in a safe space where failure costs nothing.
  2. Practise it in a simple puzzle with one clear solution.
  3. Combine it with a mechanic the player already knows.
  4. Master it in a puzzle that needs both, for an earned "aha".

What it Teaches: Steering the boat while aiming the flashlight, using sound to locate the monster and spotlights to find the way.

What the Player Sees First: A short cutscene frames the monster and shows the flashlight driving it back, so players know both the threat and the tool before they take control.


Intended Solution:

  1. Steer the boat and aim the flashlight.
  2. Listen for where the monster appears.
  3. Keep the light on the monster while steering toward the next spotlight.

How the Space Guides: Spotlights mark the safe route, so the path is always visible without any text.

On Failure: The player returns to the start of the section with no other penalty, in line with the Gentle Mastery pillar.
For an all-ages game, playtesting is everything: what looks obvious to a designer can stump a first-time player. I planned and ran the playtests and turned what we saw into design changes.

blocks.text: Iteration Case 1: Puzzle Players Couldn't See

blocks.html:
Problem: In one Act II puzzle, testers kept missing a key interaction point. Only ~70% solved it; the rest got stuck, lost the story's momentum, and some left the session early.

Cause: The camera and sightlines pulled attention away from the object players needed, and nothing in the space pointed to it.


Options Considered:

  • Add an on-screen prompt. Rejected: it breaks the no-text pillar and gives the answer away.
  • Make the object glow constantly. Rejected: it removes the discovery and looks out of place in the art style.
  • Change how the space presents it. Chosen: it fixes the problem where it started.


Fix: I reframed the camera to bring the objective into view, adjusted sightlines in the blockout with level design, and added lighting cues that lead the eye without spelling out the answer.

Result: The solve rate rose from ~70% to ~90%, and the "aha" moment stayed intact.

• No Text Tutorials: Teaching through space took far more design and testing time than a prompt would have, but it kept the story wordless and the pillars intact.
  • Forgiving Controls Over Precision: Generous tolerances meant puzzles could never rely on precise platforming; challenge had to come from understanding, not dexterity.

• Released on Steam, November 2020 - 93% positive reviews
  • Winner, Best Game for Social Impact, Games for Change Latin America 2020
  • Finalist, Impact category, BIG Festival 2021
  • Act II puzzles reached 80% solve rates without outside help by the final playtest round

What Worked
  • Teaching through space instead of text kept the story intact and worked for players of all ages.
  • Testing early with first-time players found problems the team could no longer see.

What I'd do Differently
  • Set measurable targets, such as solve rate and time per puzzle, before the first playtest rather than during.
  • Test the camera with first-time players earlier, since many later fixes were camera fixes.

What I Learned
  • For young or new players, the camera does most of the teaching.
  • What seems obvious to a designer often isn't; test early with people who have never seen the game.
